intro: A hen’s clucking grows into repeated chords and running passages in Rameau’s La Poule, played here by Marcelle Meyer on piano. The bird starts on a single G.

sections.label: A · The hen clucks on G
sections.mNote: Repeated Gs grow into chords and quick runs

sections.label: A′ · The clucking starts again on D
sections.mNote: The repeated-note figure begins the second half in D minor

sections.label: Coda · Runs descend into G minor
sections.mNote: The bass runs down beneath the final chord

cues.title: A hen on one G
cues.text: The right hand repeats G, then flicks upwards. Rameau prints “co co co co co” beneath the opening notes. The left hand joins the clucking, and the little flourish begins to climb higher.
cues.evidence: Rameau, La Poule, in Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin (c. 1728), Saint-Saëns edition (Durand, 1895), p. 86: repeated Gs and the printed clucking syllables. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meyer at Salle Adyar
cues.text: Paris, October 1953: Marcelle Meyer records Rameau’s three harpsichord books at Salle Adyar, playing them on the piano. La Poule belongs to the third book, alongside dances, Les Sauvages and L’Enharmonique.
cues.evidence: Classical Pianists chronology, Marcelle Meyer, session MaMe-C#015, lists the Rameau recordings on 29–30 October 1953 at Salle Adyar: https://classical-pianists.net/viii/marcelle-meyer/chronology/. The Nouvelles Suites score gives the contents of the third book.

cues.title: One note becomes a chord
cues.text: The repeated-note figure keeps acquiring companions. Sometimes one line clucks alone; elsewhere both hands repeat chords beneath a longer upper note. Rameau marks exchanges of fort and doux — loud and soft — across the piece.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 86–89: single-note figures, repeated chords, held upper notes and fort/doux markings.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The hen starts on D
cues.text: The second half begins with the clucking figure on D, after a cadence in D minor. The same quick upward flick sets off another stretch of repeated notes and runs, now working back towards G minor.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 87–89: D minor cadence and double bar, repeated Ds at the start of the second half, then the eventual G minor close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass makes its descent
cues.text: Near the end, repeated notes trade places between the hands while quick runs sweep across them. The last G minor chord stays above a descending bass run, which carries the piano down to a low G.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 89, final systems: exchanges of repeated notes and runs, then a held G minor chord over the descending bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: D minor starts another round
transitions.from: A · The hen clucks on G
transitions.to: A′ · The clucking starts again on D
transitions.how: The first half closes in D minor, with the bass running down beneath the held chord. After the double bar, the right hand alone repeats D and adds the familiar upward flick. The left hand re-enters as the figure climbs.
transitions.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 87–88: D minor cadence, double bar, repeated Ds and renewed accompaniment. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf

transitions.title: Clucking and runs converge on G
transitions.from: A′ · The clucking starts again on D
transitions.to: Coda · Runs descend into G minor
transitions.how: The piano exchanges repeated notes between high and low parts, with quick runs crossing them. The final phrase settles into G minor. Its upper chord holds while the bass runs down to G.
transitions.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 89, final systems: repeated-note exchanges, G minor cadence and descending bass. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf

fields.note: The hosted item is La Poule alone, not the whole suite. The collection is conventionally dated about 1728; this is an approximate publication date, not a documented composition day. composer.epithet: He explained the roots of chords in a treatise, then sent them through hell in his first opera, at fifty.
facts: Organist in Dijon, Clermont-Ferrand and Lyon; first harpsichord book, 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
Alexandre Le Riche de La Pouplinière, financier with a private orchestra
composer.background:
When Hippolyte et Aricie opened at the Paris Opéra on 1 October 1733, Rameau had just turned fifty. The singers and players had already defeated one of its boldest pages: a trio for the Fates whose lurching harmonies proved too difficult in rehearsal and had to be cut. The rest was quite enough to divide the house. Admirers heard a new theatrical voice; devotees of Lully heard an attack on their inheritance. An organist from Dijon had arrived with a first opera and a great deal of music to get off his chest.

His father played the organ in Dijon. Jean-Philippe followed the trade through a succession of French churches, with appointments in Clermont-Ferrand, Dijon and Lyon and an early attempt to establish himself in Paris. There he published his first harpsichord book in 1706. It begins with an unmeasured prelude: notes whose timing the player must work out, followed by a faster section that suddenly acquires a regular beat. Allemandes, courante and sarabandes follow. He was twenty-three, writing within the French keyboard tradition before Couperin had published his first book.
